reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it tests a purported Adopt Me game-pass glitch, demonstrates the proposed chat-code method, and then states that the method is fake and that people claiming it works are scammers. The video also promotes separate in-game giveaways conditioned on subscribing, liking, and enabling notifications, but the main communicative action is debunking the free-game-pass claim rather than directing viewers into a deceptive claim or verification flow.

opening.argument: The title promises viewers they can get any Adopt Me game pass for free, and the description makes watching the video the condition: “All you have to do is watch the video!” The video then presents a chat-code-and-reset procedure as a way to obtain game passes without Robux. That is a concrete free-asset promise tied to viewer participation, not merely discussion of game passes. The fact that the video later says the method failed does not erase the solicitation established by its headline and instructions.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Testing a claim and eventually calling it fake does not change what viewers were first promised or shown how to try. The method is described in actionable steps, including entering a string and resetting; the video’s later failure report cannot establish that the initial free-game-pass pitch was harmless to viewers who acted on it.

opening.argument: The strongest risk signal is the promise of a valuable in-game asset for no Robux, paired with a supposed bypass of the ordinary purchase flow. The video says the game pass costs 250 Robux, then presents a purported glitch that would make it free, using a chat entry and character reset. It also asks giveaway entrants to comment their Roblox username in exchange for a free pet. These claims combine easy rewards with actions from viewers; the material does not establish what happens to usernames or whether the giveaway is fulfilled, but the combination warrants treating the solicitation cautiously.

opening.argument: Although framed as an investigation, the video also functions as promotion for a free-reward proposition. Its headline promises any game pass for free, its description says watching is enough, and the narration spends time presenting a supposed procedure viewers can reproduce. At the end, the speaker pivots to a separate free-pet giveaway and asks viewers to subscribe, enable notifications, and like the video. The debunking may be genuine, but that framing also attracts viewers with free assets and channels them toward engagement-based participation.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the video an investigation accounts for its ending, but not its promotional packaging or the audience actions attached to the other reward. It advertises free game passes up front, walks through the alleged method, and closes by soliciting subscriptions, notifications, and likes for a giveaway. The warning is part of the presentation, but it does not make those reward-linked requests disappear.
